problem_framing.rationale: The decision is framed exactly as posed (raise or not, where, by how much). The 15% ARR and >100% NRR objectives are used as explicit pass/fail tests in the options comparison. The renewal-timing and enterprise-contract constraint is central to the analysis. Five sub-questions name the issues the answer turns on (where churn rises, who will pay, what each option adds). One blemish: a low-cost SMB tier and new-customer growth are declared out of scope 'by agreement at the brief', which the pack does not support. The exclusion is transparent and reasoned, so I penalise it under judgment rather than here.

storyline_coherence.rationale: The governing thought answers the question, the five summary points map one-to-one to the sections, and almost every title is a claim backed by its slide. Reading the titles alone gives the argument. Flaws: heavy redundancy (slides 5/6/8/9/10 and 18–23 restate the same points); section dividers all carry the first section's title; slide 35's title does not match its content. There is also an internal inconsistency: the CFO plan is said to 'miss' at three times the 2023 reaction, while the backup shows it at $99.03M, above target.

evidence_and_reasoning.rationale: I re-derived every key figure and all are correct. Blended logo churn is 1.71%→2.62% and ARR-weighted 0.83%→1.19%. Implied promotion-cohort churn is 4.9%, with 91% of the SMB rise due to mix. The reachable uplift is $7.57M with a correct waterfall. Break-even is 10.7% against a 3.6% 2023 reaction. Weighted NRR is 109.3%, giving $93.98M, $99.03M and $99.37M. The sensitivities also check. All critical evidence is used, including evidence against the plan (test covered new sign-ups at 10%; 2023 predates Inkwell). Derivations and assumptions are transparent. It falls short of 5 on three points. The headline 'Mid-market has shown it will pay more' overstates a non-significant new-sign-up test. 'At least $99.03M whatever SMB customers do' ignores that SMB churn feeds the NRR assumption. The verdict that the CFO plan 'misses' at about 3x contradicts the document's own $99.03M figure. The out-of-scope 'agreement at the brief' is invented.

strategic_judgment.rationale: The recommendation is clear, segment-differentiated and follows from the analysis. Three options are compared on the stated criteria. There is a gated SMB test with a decision rule, a mid-market fallback, guardrails with breach responses, named owners, and sensitivities showing where the plan breaks. It avoids all five traps and revises the CFO hypothesis appropriately. Gaps: (1) The SMB response to Inkwell (lower tier or packaging) is scoped out on an invented basis, so the compete-versus-monetise trade-off is only partly addressed. (2) The plan clears the target by only $0.13M before new customers, and the stated mid-market fallback to 10% would put the existing-base figure below target (about $98.3M), which is not flagged. (3) Mid-market is taken to 12%, beyond the tested 10% and on renewals, apparently because the target needs it. (4) The CFO plan's downside is overstated. (5) Customer trust at renewal is barely discussed.

clarity_and_concision.rationale: The answer is on the summary slide and the language is plain and precise. But at 43 slides and about 6,400 words it is substantially longer than the decision needs. Section-overview slides restate the detail slides, dividers repeat, and several backup slides duplicate the body. The CEO could get the same decision from roughly a third of the length.

unsupported_claims.quote: Mid-market has shown it will pay more
unsupported_claims.why: The only evidence is a three-month test on new sign-ups at +10% with a non-significant difference. Renewing customers at +12% are untested, as the document itself concedes elsewhere.

unsupported_claims.quote: About $99.4M; at least $99.03M whatever SMB customers do
unsupported_claims.why: The floor depends on holding trailing NRR at 109.3% and on zero mid-market reaction. SMB churn from Inkwell, independent of price, would lower NRR, and the document's own sensitivity shows a 1-point slip misses the target.

unsupported_claims.quote: Three branches were left out on purpose, two by agreement at the brief and one because we cannot move it
unsupported_claims.why: The pack contains no agreement that a low-cost SMB tier or new-customer growth is out of scope. The scope limit is invented.

unsupported_claims.quote: Price drove the promotion cohort out, not the core base
unsupported_claims.why: This is a causal claim from exit surveys in which 48% of promotion leavers did not cite price. Low activation is an equally supported cause, and the pack lists whether the cohort 'will mostly churn regardless' as an open uncertainty.

logical_contradictions.quote_a: 12% on every plan (CFO): About $100.7M if SMB reacts as in 2023; misses if it reacts about three times as strongly
logical_contradictions.quote_b: CFO plan, SMB reaction at break-even: $99.03M; SMB gain fully lost to churn
logical_contradictions.why: Break-even is the three-times-2023 reaction. On the document's own numbers the CFO plan then delivers $99.03M, which is above the $98.9M target, so it does not miss at about 3x. It would need more than about 3.1x (about 11.3% extra loss).

recommendation.summary: Raise mid-market 12% at renewal and enterprise 7% where capped and 12% where uncapped from January 2027. Hold SMB prices pending a randomised Q1 test of +8% on non-promotion renewals, with a July decision gated at 0.5 pp extra churn. Hold the promotion cohort's price through 2027 and run activation onboarding. Agree one churn definition for the board.
recommendation.rationale: It meets all four defensibility criteria. It separates mix from rate (4.9% against 2.1%, 91% of the rise). It reconciles the CFO and CEO views: the rise is a promotion-cohort effect, but price matters for that cohort and Inkwell makes SMB pricing unproven. It corrects the $10.3M to $7.57M. It differentiates by segment, with a staged SMB test and churn guardrails.

hypothesis_handling.rationale: The document keeps the CFO's 12% for mid-market and uncapped enterprise but rejects the uniform increase. It corrects the $10.3M to $7.6M and holds SMB pending a test because Inkwell post-dates the 2023 precedent. It supports 'churn is mostly not a core-base price problem' with the mix decomposition and the survey split by cohort, while accepting the CEO's concern for SMB. It also challenges the Customer Success 'halve churn' claim, capping it at 32%, and flags the undefined dashboard metric. The one causal overreach is 'price drove the promotion cohort out', where activation is an equally supported cause.

output.overall_comment: Analytically very strong. Every required calculation is done and correct, all critical evidence is used and cohort-split, the CFO's hypothesis is revised rather than accepted or rejected wholesale, and the recommendation is a gated, segment-differentiated plan with guardrails, owners and sensitivities. Main weaknesses: a few overstated headlines (mid-market 'has shown it will pay more'; the floor holds 'whatever SMB customers do'); an inconsistency in how the CFO option's downside is described; an invented scope exclusion that sidelines the SMB packaging response to Inkwell; a thin $0.13M margin over target, where the stated mid-market fallback to 10% would fall short on the existing base; and length, at 43 slides with much repetition. Weighted score is about 4.05.
